package.title: How Desert Ice Houses Worked 2,400 Years Ago
package.description:
How did ancient people make ice in the desert without electricity? A yakhchal was an ancient Persian ice house: shaded pools froze on clear winter nights, and a giant thick-walled cone stored the ice all summer.

In this Short: the shade wall, the night-sky freezing trick, and how the cone kept ice cold through a desert summer.

Sources:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakhch%C4%81l
https://www.birdsoutsidemywindow.org/2021/01/06/how-to-make-ice-in-the-desert/
https://www.historicmysteries.com/yakhchal/
tags: how did ancient people make ice
package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: the walls were made of a special mortar mixed with sand, clay, lime, ash, egg whites and even goat hair. What ancient invention should we animate next?

key_facts: Ancient Persians engineered ice houses known as yakhchals over 2,400 years ago without electricity.
Water was channeled from underground aqueducts (qanats) into long, shallow outdoor basins.
A massive, tall adobe wall shielded the shallow pools from solar radiation throughout the day.
Through radiative cooling, the water shed heat directly into the clear, dry night sky and froze during winter nights.
Ice blocks were harvested and moved into an enormous, thick-walled mudbrick cone.
Thermal convection allowed warm air to escape through a top apex vent while cold, dense air sank into a deep subterranean pit.
Layered with insulating straw, stored ice remained frozen through extreme desert summer heat.

The oldest message in a bottle ever found was thrown from the German ship Paula in 1886 and found on a beach in Western Australia in 2018. This message in a bottle spent 131 years lost before anyone read it.

package.title: How 2,000-Year-Old Concrete Seals Cracks
package.description:
Ancient Roman concrete was self-healing concrete, and here's how Roman concrete works. Hot-mixed quicklime left white lime lumps inside, and when a crack hits one, water turns the lime back into stone and seals it.

In this Short: the hot-mixing trick, the white lumps everyone thought were mistakes, and how a crack seals itself in about two weeks.

Sources:
https://www.sci.news/archaeology/ancient-roman-concrete-mystery-11553.html
https://www.dezeen.com/2023/01/17/self-healing-roman-concrete-mit-harvard/amp/
https://www.designboom.com/architecture/ancient-roman-concrete-durable-mit-self-healing-abilities-01-09-2023/
tags: why roman concrete is so strong
package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: the samples in the study came from the city wall of Privernum, an ancient city near Rome. What ancient invention should we animate next?
package.visual_bible: A cohesive stylized 3D animation juxtaposing modern cool-gray concrete sidewalk slabs with warm, sunlit sand-colored ancient Roman mortar walls featuring chalky white lime clasts and clear cross-section cutaways under soft cinematic sunlight.
key_facts: Roman builders hot-mixed quicklime with volcanic ash and water.
The intense heat of hot-mixing left small, brittle white lime clasts inside the concrete.
Historically, researchers assumed these lime clasts were the result of poor or sloppy mixing.
When cracks propagate through Roman concrete, they naturally travel directly through the weaker lime clasts.
Infiltrating rainwater dissolves calcium from the exposed lime clasts, forming a calcium-saturated solution.
The calcium solution recrystallizes into solid calcium carbonate (limestone), sealing the crack.
Laboratory tests demonstrated these cracks self-healed within approximately two weeks.

In 1916, the Bank of Vernal in Utah had its brick front mailed brick by brick, because parcel post was cheaper than freight. Here is the true story of the parcel post bank and how it changed post office rules.

package.title: How A Click Pen Works in 2 Clicks
package.description:
Here's how a click pen works, step by step inside the barrel. The retractable pen mechanism is just a plunger, a tiny rotating cam and a spring, and this click pen mechanism locks the tip out on one click and pulls it back in on the next.

In this Short: the toothed plunger, the crown-shaped cam that twists a step each click, the ledge that locks the tip out, and the gap that lets it retract.

Sources:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retractable_pen
https://benlauengr.commons.gc.cuny.edu/?p=106
https://makezine.com/article/craft/retractable-pen-work/
tags: how a retractable ballpoint pen works
package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: the designer of one famous click pen says it took a team of sixty-six people to design. Do you click your pen when you're thinking, or is that just us?
package.visual_bible: A minimalist white studio desktop setting featuring a translucent royal-blue plastic retractable ballpoint pen with precision-molded white internal cam parts and a polished steel spring, rendered in crisp 3D technical animation under soft studio lighting.
key_facts: A retractable click pen operates using a plunger, a crown-shaped rotating cam, and a spring.
The plunger has straight teeth that mesh with slanted teeth on the cam.
The angled teeth force the cam to rotate a step each time the plunger presses down.
Releasing the plunger allows the spring to push the cam onto an internal barrel ledge, locking the pen tip out.
A second click forces the cam off the ledge and twists it into alignment with vertical channels.
The spring pulls the ink cartridge and tip back inside the barrel when aligned with the channels.
A full extend-and-retract cycle takes two clicks and two cam rotations.

package.title: 30 Cats vs a Square Made of Nothing 😂
package.description:
Cats sit in squares that aren't even there, and a 2021 cat study tested it. In this "if I fits I sits" experiment, 30 cats were shown a fake square made of paper Pac-Man shapes - an optical illusion - next to a real one.

In this Short: the paper Pac-Man illusion, the owners in sunglasses, and what the cats actually did.

Sources:

key_facts: In 2021, researchers published a citizen science experiment testing domestic cats with the Kanizsa square visual illusion.
The illusion uses four circular shapes with wedges removed resembling Pac-Man, arranged so human and animal brains perceive a phantom square contour.
Cat owners were instructed to wear sunglasses indoors during trials to avoid involuntary eye-gaze cueing.
Hundreds of owners enrolled, but only 30 cats completed all daily testing protocols.
Cats chose to sit inside the illusory Kanizsa square just as frequently as inside an actual taped square outline.

package.title: How Archimedes' Screw Works (2,200 Years Old)
package.description:
Here's how an Archimedes screw works, step by step inside the tube. This ancient water pump lifts water uphill with no motor: each turn of the spiral traps a pocket of water and carries it up.

In this Short: the spiral inside the tube, the scooped pocket, why the water's low point climbs as it turns, why too steep a tilt spills it, and where these screws are still used.

Sources:
https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/lift-water-with-an-archimedes-screw
https://www.sciencebuddies.org/stem-activities/build-archimedes-screw
https://greekreporter.com/2025/03/29/archimedes-screw-ancient-greek-invention-used-today/
package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: some modern Archimedes screws run in reverse, letting water fall down them to spin a generator. If you had to lift water without a motor, how would you do it?
package.visual_bible: Sunny daytime setting featuring a rustic wooden Archimedes screw tube with clear water elements set alongside a calm blue river with warm earth tones and realistic materials.

scenes.text: You can't pour water uphill, but you could with a two-thousand-year-old screw. How?

scenes.text: It's a spiral sealed inside a tube, tilted into a river.

scenes.image_prompt: 3D cutaway animation of a transparent cylinder revealing an internal wooden helical spiral blade wrapped around a center axis, technical illustration, 8k
scenes.shot: 3D animated cutaway of the same wooden tube turning see-through to reveal a thick wooden spiral wound around a central shaft inside, camera gliding along the tube from bottom to top
scenes.stock_query: spiral screw inside pipe cross section

scenes.text: Turn it, and the bottom scoops a pocket of water.
scenes.image_prompt: 3D macro underwater shot of the base of a rotating wooden spiral scooping a clear pocket of water into its chamber, ray-traced lighting
scenes.shot: 3D animated close-up of the same tube's bottom end underwater: the crank turns, the lowest blade of the spiral dips and scoops a small pocket of bright blue water, camera locked off

scenes.text: The water rolls to the lowest point of its turn.
scenes.image_prompt: 3D cross-section macro view of a single turn of an Archimedes screw with water gathered naturally at the lowest bottom curve, crisp details
scenes.shot: 3D animated cross-section macro of one turn of the same spiral: the blue water pocket settles in the lowest curve of the blade like a marble in a bowl, slow orbit

scenes.text: But as the screw spins, that low point creeps upward.

scenes.text: So the water climbs, pocket after pocket.

scenes.image_prompt: Full cutaway 3D view of an Archimedes screw tube showing several distinct chambers of blue water ascending like steps along the spiral, photorealistic render
scenes.shot: 3D animated full-length cutaway of the same tube: a staircase of separate blue water pockets rises turn by turn, each resting on the blade beneath it, camera slowly pulling back

scenes.text: Too steep, and it spills back down.
scenes.image_prompt: 3D cross-section demonstration of an overly steep Archimedes screw where trapped water overflows the blade edge and splashes downward, dynamic fluids
scenes.shot: 3D animated comparison of the same tube tilted much steeper: the blue pockets slosh over the blades and slide back down to the river, camera side-on

scenes.text: At the top, every turn pours out a splash.

scenes.shot: 3D animated close-up of the same tube's top end: with each turn of the crank a splash of blue water pours into a wooden trough, slow-motion droplets

scenes.text: Plants still use giant ones, because even now,

scenes.shot: 3D animated wide shot dissolving from the same wooden screw to a huge modern steel screw turning in a concrete channel, then back to the calm river and the tilted wooden tube, gentle push-in

key_facts: An Archimedes screw lifts liquid uphill without a pressurized motor.
It consists of a helical spiral enclosed tightly within a cylinder placed at an incline.
Rotating the screw scoops a isolated pocket of water at the base.
Gravity keeps the water at the lowest point of each turn, which physically shifts upward as the screw rotates.
If the angle of tilt is too steep, the water slips over the blades and fails to rise.
Modern wastewater treatment and drainage plants still utilize large Archimedes screws today.

package.description:
This is the true story of how the sailing stones move: the moving rocks of Racetrack Playa in Death Valley. For seventy years nobody knew, until GPS trackers caught thin ice and wind pushing them in 2013.

In this Short: the mystery trails, the fifteen GPS rocks, the frozen pond, and how ice and a light breeze moved the stones.

This is a true story.

package.script: You'd think rocks can't move by themselves. In Death Valley, they left tracks hundreds of feet long. Here's the true story of how scientists finally caught them moving. package.title: How Zippers Work in 2 Moves
package.description:
How does a zipper work? Here's how zippers work, step by step inside the slider. A zipper slider has a Y-shaped tunnel that squeezes two rows of teeth together so every bump locks into a hollow, then a wedge pries them apart when you pull it down.

In this Short: the bump-and-hollow shape of zipper teeth, how the slider's Y-shaped tunnel locks them, why a closed zipper won't split sideways, and how the wedge unzips it.

Sources:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zipper
https://blog.ncf-india.org/saw/zippers-how-do-they-work
package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: the name "zipper" came from B.F. Goodrich in 1923, which used it on rubber boots. Has a zipper ever split on you right in the middle?

scenes.text: You zip your jacket every day, but do you know what's happening inside that tiny slider?

scenes.text: Pull up, and a Y-shaped tunnel squeezes both rows together.

scenes.shot: 3D animated cutaway of the same silver slider turning see-through to reveal a Y-shaped tunnel inside, the two open rows of teeth feeding into the two arms of the Y as the slider moves up, camera locked from above

scenes.text: The teeth meet tilted, so each bump slips past.

scenes.shot: 3D animated cross-section inside the same slider: two teeth from opposite rows enter tilted at an angle, one tooth's bump sliding past the edge of the tooth beside it, slow motion

scenes.text: Then they straighten, and every bump snaps into a hollow.
scenes.image_prompt: 3D animated cross-section of the same teeth reaching the straight bottom of the Y tunnel: they flatten into a line and each bump clicks into the hollow of the next tooth, small spark of light at each click
scenes.shot: 3D animated cross-section of the same teeth reaching the straight bottom of the Y tunnel: they flatten into a line and each bump clicks into the hollow of the next tooth, small spark of light at each click

scenes.text: Now it's one locked chain.

scenes.text: Pull down, and a tiny wedge tilts them apart.

scenes.shot: 3D animated cutaway of the same slider moving down: a small triangle-shaped wedge in the middle of the Y pushes between the locked teeth and tilts them back to an angle, camera tracking down

scenes.text: The bumps pop free, one by one.
scenes.image_prompt: 3D animated macro of the same row of teeth separating one after another as the slider passes, each bump popping out of its hollow with a tiny bounce, camera gliding alongside
scenes.shot: 3D animated macro of the same row of teeth separating one after another as the slider passes, each bump popping out of its hollow with a tiny bounce, camera gliding alongside

scenes.text: The trick is the slider, hidden every time
scenes.image_prompt: 3D animated close-up dissolving from the see-through slider back to the shiny silver slider on the blue jacket, pull tab swinging gently, slow push-in
scenes.shot: 3D animated close-up dissolving from the see-through slider back to the shiny silver slider on the blue jacket, pull tab swinging gently, slow push-in

A zipper slider features a Y-shaped tunnel that squeezes the two rows of teeth together.

Why do dogs tilt their heads when you talk? A 2021 study of forty dogs found genius word-learning dogs tilt their heads far more often when you say a toy's name.

In this Short: the Hungarian study, genius border collies vs regular dogs, the 43 percent vs 2 percent result, and why each dog has a favorite tilt side.

https://ttkold.elte.hu/en/content/talk-to-tilt-head-tilting-in-dogs.t.5018

package.title: How 1 Pie Tin Became the Frisbee 🥧
package.description:
Why is it called a Frisbee? Frisbee history starts with a pie: the Frisbee is named after the Frisbie Pie Company of Bridgeport, Connecticut, whose empty pie tins college students tossed across campus.

In this Short: the pie tins at Yale, Fred Morrison's Pluto Platter, how Wham-O renamed it the Frisbee, and what happened to the bakery.

This is a true story.

topic.title: Why do leaves turn orange in fall?
topic.angle: Low-Poly Faceted

package.title: Why Do Leaves Turn Orange in Fall? 🍂
package.description:
Why do leaves change color in autumn? The yellow and orange carotenoid pigments are in the leaf all summer, hidden by green chlorophyll, and show through when the tree stops making chlorophyll and pulls nutrients back before the leaf falls.

Sources:
https://www.fs.usda.gov/media/217554
https://earthwiseradio.org/2012/10/autumn-leaves-not-just-a-colorful-display/
https://thesca.org/newsroom/why-leaves-change-color-fall

Animated in the Low-Poly Faceted style.
package.pinned_comment: Which tree turns the brightest where you live? Maples win on my street 🍁
package.script:
Why do leaves turn orange in fall?
Here's the twist:
the orange was there all summer.
A leaf is packed with green chlorophyll,
the pigment that turns sunlight into sugar.
But it's also holding yellow and orange pigments,
called carotenoids.
All summer, the green drowns them out.
Then the nights get longer,
and the tree shuts the leaf down.
It stops making chlorophyll,
and breaks the old green apart.
Scientists think it pulls back about half the leaf's nitrogen,
saving it for spring.
With the green gone,
the hidden orange shows through.
And the reds?
Those are brand new.
Trapped sugars turn into red pigments,
right before a cork-like seal forms at the stem,
and the leaf lets go.
So fall doesn't paint the leaves.
It peels the green away.
Which tree turns the brightest where you live?
key_facts: Yellow/orange carotenoids are in leaves all year, masked by more abundant green chlorophyll (USDA Forest Service)
In fall, shorter days and cooler temps make trees stop replacing chlorophyll, so the green fades (USDA Forest Service)
Red pigments are newly formed in fall from sugars trapped in the leaf (USDA Forest Service)
A layer of cork cells forms at the base of the leaf stalk and the leaf falls (USDA Forest Service)
Trees pull back roughly half or more of the leaf's nitrogen before it drops; a fallen leaf keeps ~40% of its summer nitrogen (EarthWise)

package.title: How Romans Heated Their Floors 2,000 Years Ago
package.description:
How did the ancient Romans heat their floors without electricity? The hypocaust raised the floor on stacks of bricks called pilae, so hot air from a wood furnace could flow underneath and up hollow clay pipes in the walls, turning the whole bathhouse into a radiator.

Chapters:
0:00 Warm floors 2,000 years ago
0:21 Who invented the hypocaust
0:40 How it worked
1:46 Vitruvius' oddly specific rule
2:18 How hot it got
2:47 After Rome, and today

Sources:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypocaust
https://lexundria.com/vitr/5.10.2/mg
https://www.carnuntum.at/tr/dergi/the-floor-is-lava-heiztechniken-im-antiken-carnuntum/1723

Animated in the Claymation Set style.

Follow Zorbly AI for a new Short every day.
package.pinned_comment: Would you swap your radiator for a Roman hypocaust floor, if someone else did the wood shoveling? 🔥
package.script:
How did the Romans heat their floors,
without a single wire?
Two thousand years ago,
in the middle of winter,
a Roman could walk across a stone floor barefoot,
and it would be warm.
The trick was hiding under their feet.
It's called a hypocaust,
which means "heat from below."
The Roman writer Vitruvius
credits a businessman named Sergius Orata,
around 95 BC.
Orata got rich farming oysters,
and he sold wealthy Romans on heated "hanging baths."
Soon, no fancy villa was complete without one.
So how did it work?
Start with a furnace,
called the praefurnium,
built just outside the room, a little lower down.
Slaves fed it wood all day.
Now, instead of laying the floor on the ground,
the Romans lifted it up.
They built short stacks of square bricks,
called pilae,
row after row.
Vitruvius says two feet tall.
On top went big two-foot tiles,
then a thick layer of concrete,
then the floor you'd walk on.
That left a hollow space underneath,
like a crawl space made for smoke.
The fire's hot air and smoke
rushed into that gap,
swirled between the pillars,
and soaked heat into the floor above.
But it didn't stop there.
Hollow clay pipes, called tubuli,
ran up inside the walls.
Hot air climbed through them,
warming the walls too,
then escaped through vents near the roof.
So the whole room became a radiator.
Here's a detail Vitruvius was oddly specific about.
The floor underneath should slope toward the furnace,
so if you threw a ball in,
it couldn't stop inside.
It would roll right back to the fire.
Romans also lined up their rooms by heat.
The caldarium, the hot room,
sat closest to the furnace.
Next came the warm room,
the tepidarium.
And the cold plunge pool, the frigidarium,
sat farthest away.
So, how hot did it get?
In modern tests on rebuilt Roman baths,
the floors reached twenty to fifty degrees Celsius.
Hot enough that bathers wore wooden-soled sandals.
The hot room's air sat around thirty-two degrees,
thick with steam.
And all of it ran on wood.
The giant Baths of Caracalla in Rome
reportedly burned around ten tons of wood,
every single day.
When the empire fell apart,
so did the skills and the labor
that kept these furnaces burning.
For centuries,
much of Europe went back to smoky open fires.
But the idea never died.
In Korea, the ondol system
runs fire smoke under the floor in a very similar way.
And today's underfloor heating
does exactly what the Romans did:
warm the floor,
and let the heat rise.
Just with pipes instead of pillars,
and nobody shoveling wood.
Would you trade your radiator
for a Roman floor?
key_facts: Hypocaust = 'heat from below': floor raised on pilae so furnace (praefurnium) gases flow underneath (Wikipedia: Hypocaust, Praefurnium)
Vitruvius credits Sergius Orata (fl. c. 95 BC), an oyster farmer who popularised 'hanging baths'; attribution not fully established (Wikipedia: Sergius Orata)
Vitruvius 5.10.2: pillars two feet high topped with two-foot tiles; the underfloor slopes to the furnace so a thrown ball rolls back out
Hollow clay tubuli in the walls carried hot air up and out (Wikipedia: Praefurnium; vita-romae.com)
Reconstruction experiments: floors 20-50 C, walls up to 30 C, caldarium air ~32 C and very humid (Carnuntum)
Baths of Caracalla reportedly burned ~10 tons of wood a day; hypocausts declined with the Western Empire (WorldAtlas)
Korean ondol routes fire smoke under the floor in a similar way; modern underfloor heating uses pipes

00:00:55,160 --> 00:00:57,230
the Romans lifted it up.

23
00:00:57,780 --> 00:00:59,980
They built short stacks of square bricks,

24
00:01:00,280 --> 00:01:01,280
called pilae,

25
00:01:01,580 --> 00:01:03,070
row after row.

26
00:01:03,620 --> 00:01:05,980
Vitruvius says two feet tall.

27
00:01:06,530 --> 00:01:08,860
On top went big two-foot tiles,

28
00:01:09,160 --> 00:01:11,280
then a thick layer of concrete,

29
00:01:11,580 --> 00:01:13,710
then the floor you'd walk on.

30
00:01:14,260 --> 00:01:16,700
That left a hollow space underneath,

31
00:01:17,000 --> 00:01:19,450
like a crawl space made for smoke.

32
00:01:20,000 --> 00:01:22,130
The fire's hot air and smoke

33
00:01:22,430 --> 00:01:23,890
rushed into that gap,

34
00:01:24,190 --> 00:01:25,820
swirled between the pillars,

35
00:01:26,120 --> 00:01:28,600
and soaked heat into the floor above.

36
00:01:29,150 --> 00:01:30,480
But it didn't stop there.

37
00:01:31,030 --> 00:01:33,410
Hollow clay pipes, called tubuli,

38
00:01:33,710 --> 00:01:35,760
ran up inside the walls.

39
00:01:36,310 --> 00:01:38,180
Hot air climbed through them,

40
00:01:38,480 --> 00:01:40,120
warming the walls too,

41
00:01:40,420 --> 00:01:42,950
then escaped through vents near the roof.

42
00:01:43,500 --> 00:01:46,110
So the whole room became a radiator.

43
00:01:46,660 --> 00:01:50,360
Here's a detail Vitruvius was oddly specific about.

44
00:01:50,910 --> 00:01:53,990
The floor underneath should slope toward the furnace,

45
00:01:54,290 --> 00:01:56,140
so if you threw a ball in,

46
00:01:56,440 --> 00:01:58,070
it couldn't stop inside.

47
00:01:58,620 --> 00:02:00,920
It would roll right back to the fire.

48
00:02:01,470 --> 00:02:04,510
Romans also lined up their rooms by heat.

49
00:02:05,060 --> 00:02:07,070
The caldarium, the hot room,

50
00:02:07,370 --> 00:02:09,250
sat closest to the furnace.

51
00:02:09,800 --> 00:02:11,490
Next came the warm room,

52
00:02:11,790 --> 00:02:13,050
the tepidarium.

53
00:02:13,600 --> 00:02:16,440
And the cold plunge pool, the frigidarium,

54
00:02:16,740 --> 00:02:18,170
sat farthest away.

55
00:02:18,720 --> 00:02:20,440
So, how hot did it get?

56
00:02:20,990 --> 00:02:23,920
In modern tests on rebuilt Roman baths,

57
00:02:24,220 --> 00:02:27,440
the floors reached twenty to fifty degrees Celsius.

58
00:02:27,990 --> 00:02:31,240
Hot enough that bathers wore wooden-soled sandals.

59
00:02:31,790 --> 00:02:35,010
The hot room's air sat around thirty-two degrees,

60
00:02:35,310 --> 00:02:36,530
thick with steam.

61
00:02:37,080 --> 00:02:39,070
And all of it ran on wood.

62
00:02:39,620 --> 00:02:42,350
The giant Baths of Caracalla in Rome

63
00:02:42,650 --> 00:02:45,610
reportedly burned around ten tons of wood,

64
00:02:45,910 --> 00:02:47,250
every single day.

65
00:02:47,800 --> 00:02:49,570
When the empire fell apart,

66
00:02:49,870 --> 00:02:52,200
so did the skills and the labor

67
00:02:52,500 --> 00:02:54,550
that kept these furnaces burning.

68
00:02:55,100 --> 00:02:56,160
For centuries,

69
00:02:56,460 --> 00:02:59,880
much of Europe went back to smoky open fires.

70
00:03:00,430 --> 00:03:02,460
But the idea never died.

71
00:03:03,010 --> 00:03:05,170
In Korea, the ondol system

72
00:03:05,470 --> 00:03:09,260
runs fire smoke under the floor in a very similar way.

73
00:03:09,810 --> 00:03:12,030
And today's underfloor heating

74
00:03:12,330 --> 00:03:14,820
does exactly what the Romans did:

75
00:03:15,120 --> 00:03:16,360
warm the floor,

76
00:03:16,660 --> 00:03:18,100
and let the heat rise.

77
00:03:18,650 --> 00:03:20,960
Just with pipes instead of pillars,

78
00:03:21,260 --> 00:03:23,290
and nobody shoveling wood.

79
00:03:23,840 --> 00:03:25,810
Would you trade your radiator

80
00:03:26,110 --> 00:03:27,580
for a Roman floor?

package.title: How Tape Measures Work 📏
package.description:
How do tape measures work, and why is the tape measure hook loose? See the spring that pulls the blade back, why the blade is curved, and how the wobbly hook keeps every measurement accurate.

In this Short: the coiled spring, the curved blade and the loose hook that measures inside and outside.

Sources:
https://www.engineersupply.com/How-do-measuring-tapes-work.aspx
https://www.slashgear.com/1853705/tape-measures-curved-reason/
tags: why is the tape measure hook loose
how does a tape measure retract
package.pinned_comment: Bonus: the hook moves by exactly its own thickness, so hooked or pushed, zero stays zero. Did you ever think that loose hook was broken?
package.visual_bible: Claymation-style 3D animation featuring a vibrant matte yellow tape measure with polished silver steel blade and brass rivets, set upon a rustic oak wooden workbench inside a warmly lit workshop with soft blue shadows.
key_facts: The end hook on a tape measure is intentionally loose and wobbly, not broken.
Pulling the blade winds an internal flat coiled spring around the center hub.
Releasing the blade allows the tensioned coiled spring to unwind and retract the blade automatically.
The blade is manufactured with a curved, concave cross-section that gives it structural rigidity across long spans without collapsing.
The rivets holding the hook sit in elongated slots allowing it to slide back and forth.
When hooked over an outside edge, the hook slides out by exactly its own thickness to measure from the inside face.
When pushed against an inside surface, the hook slides in by its own thickness to measure from the outside face.
This sliding mechanism ensures that both inside and outside measurements start at true zero.

package.title: The 5-Year Wait Behind Post-it Notes
package.description:
How were Post-it notes invented, and why are Post-it notes yellow? This Post-it note history starts with a failed glue in 1968 that waited five years for a use.

In this Short: the weak glue, the falling bookmark and the free samples that turned it into the sticky note.

This is a true story.

key_facts: In 1968, 3M scientist Spencer Silver invented a low-tack, reusable adhesive while trying to create a super strong glue.
The adhesive remained unused at 3M for five years.
In 1974, coworker Art Fry used the adhesive to keep bookmarks from falling out of his choir songbook.
After initial commercial failure in 1977, free sample distributions in Boise, Idaho in 1978 won consumers over.
Post-it notes officially launched across the United States in 1980.
The iconic yellow color was selected purely by chance because the adjacent laboratory only had yellow scrap paper available.

package.title: Why Your Thermos Keeps Coffee Hot for 12 Hours ☕
package.description:
How does a thermos (vacuum flask) keep coffee hot for hours? Heat escapes by conduction, convection and radiation, and a thermos blocks all three with a vacuum gap between two walls and shiny, mirror-like surfaces.

Sources:
https://www.scienceabc.com/innovation/thermos-flask-keep-hot-things-hot-cold-things-cold.html
https://www.lifeventure.com/blogs/news/vacuum-flasks-explained
https://greatpatent.com/the-thermos-was-a-laboratory-instrument-nobody-patented

package.pinned_comment: What's the longest your coffee ever stayed hot in a thermos?
package.script:
How does a thermos keep coffee hot
for twelve whole hours?
Heat escapes in three ways.
It can touch its way out,
that's conduction.
It can ride on moving air,
that's convection.
Or it can glow away as invisible light,
called radiation.
A thermos blocks all three.
It's really two bottles,
one inside the other,
and the gap between them is a vacuum.
With no air in there,
heat has nothing to touch,
and nothing to ride.
Then the walls are shiny,
like a mirror,
so the glow bounces back into your coffee.
A scientist named James Dewar
invented it in 1892,
to keep liquid gases ice cold.
The only real leak?
The lid.
So what's the longest your coffee ever stayed hot?
key_facts: Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation
A vacuum flask is two walls with a vacuum between them, which blocks conduction and convection
Silvered/shiny walls reflect infrared radiation back
Invented by Scottish scientist James Dewar in 1892 to store liquefied gases
Most remaining heat loss is through the stopper/lid
Good flasks keep drinks hot for around 12 hours

topic.title: How does a plane toilet flush at 35,000 feet?

package.title: How a Plane Toilet Flushes at 35,000 Feet ✈️
package.description:
How does an airplane toilet flush? Plane toilets are vacuum toilets: a valve opens the bowl to the thin air outside, the higher cabin pressure shoves everything into a tank at the back, and below 16,000 feet an electric vacuum pump does the job instead.

Sources:
https://satelliteindustries.com/blog/vacuum-toilet-system-in-aircraft
https://thepointsguy.com/news/how-airplane-toilets-work/
https://aerocorner.com/blog/how-airplane-toilets-work/

Animated in the Synthwave Outrun style.

Follow Zorbly AI for a new Short every day.
tags: how does a plane toilet work
package.pinned_comment: Have you ever jumped when a plane toilet flushed? Be honest 😂
package.script:
How does a plane toilet flush
at thirty-five thousand feet?
It barely uses water.
It uses the sky.
Your cabin is pressurized,
packed with air like a balloon.
Outside, the air is super thin.
Press the button,
and a valve opens a pipe
from the bowl to that thin outside air.
The high pressure in the cabin
shoves everything down the pipe.
That's the whoosh.
It all lands in a tank at the back of the plane.
About three seconds later,
the valve slams shut.
But below sixteen thousand feet,
the outside air isn't thin enough,
so an electric pump makes the vacuum instead.
And no, nothing gets dumped in the sky.
Ground crews empty the tank after landing.
So, next flight,
are you brave enough to press it?
key_facts: Airplane toilets are vacuum toilets (patented by James Kemper in 1975, on Boeing jets by 1982)
At altitude a valve connects the bowl to low outside pressure; higher cabin pressure pushes waste through
Waste goes to a tank at the rear of the aircraft
Valves close after about 3-4 seconds
Below about 16,000 ft (and on the ground) an electric vacuum generator creates the suction
Waste is not dumped in flight; ground service trucks empty the tank after landing

It's one of the longest trips in your body.
And for most of history,
nobody really knew how it worked.
Many ancient doctors thought the stomach
simply cooked your food, like a pot.
Then, in the seventeen hundreds,
scientists fed animals
food sealed inside little metal tubes.
The food couldn't be squished,
but it still dissolved.
Italian scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani
even tried it on himself,
swallowing tiny linen bags of food.
The answer was a liquid.
He called it gastric juice.
So let's follow one bite,
all the way through.
Step one: your mouth.
Your teeth crush the bite into mush,
and saliva soaks it.
Saliva holds an enzyme called amylase,
that starts turning starch into sugar,
before you even swallow.
Then your tongue pushes the food back,
and a tiny flap, the epiglottis,
folds down over your windpipe,
so nothing goes the wrong way.
Now the food enters the esophagus,
a muscle tube about twenty-five centimeters long.
It doesn't just fall.
Rings of muscle squeeze behind it,
like toothpaste in a tube.
That's called peristalsis.
The trip takes about nine seconds,
and it works even upside down.
Next stop, the stomach.
It's a stretchy bag of muscle,
filled with hydrochloric acid.
Stomach acid can drop to around pH two,
about as sour as lemon juice.
It kills a lot of germs,
and helps an enzyme called pepsin
start chopping up protein.
About three times a minute,
the stomach walls squeeze and churn,
mixing everything into a thick soup called chyme.
That can take two to four hours.
So why doesn't your stomach digest itself?
Its lining makes a thick coat of mucus,
plus bicarbonate to calm the acid.
And the lining cells get replaced every few days.
Then a little valve opens,
and lets the chyme out, a squirt at a time,
into the small intestine.
This is where the real magic happens.
It's about five meters long,
coiled up inside your belly.
Your liver sends in bile,
which breaks fat into tiny droplets.
Your pancreas adds more enzymes,
and neutralizes the acid.
The walls are covered in millions of tiny fingers,
called villi,
and those are covered in even tinier microvilli.
Spread flat, scientists estimate your gut lining
covers about thirty-two square meters.
That's half a badminton court!
Old textbooks said a whole tennis court,
but half a court is still huge.
Right here, most of the nutrients
slip into your blood.
What's left moves on to the large intestine.
It's wider, but only about one and a half meters long.
Its main job is soaking up water.
And it's home to trillions of bacteria.
Scientists estimate about thirty-eight trillion live in you,
mostly right here.
They munch the fiber you can't digest,
and make some vitamins in return.
So how long does the whole trip take?
About six hours through the stomach and small intestine,
and up to another two days in the large intestine.
Whatever your body can't use,
leaves at the end.
But the rest?
That bite became your energy,
your muscles,
even the thoughts you're having right now.
So which food do you think
takes the longest trip?
key_facts: Ancient physicians described digestion as 'concoction', a kind of cooking in the stomach; in the 1750s Réaumur fed a bird food in perforated metal tubes and the food still dissolved (Popular Science Monthly, 1909)
Lazzaro Spallanzani experimented on animals and himself in the 1770s-80s and named the stomach's solvent 'gastric juice' (whonamedit; Popular Science Monthly)
Saliva's amylase starts breaking starch into sugar; the epiglottis covers the windpipe during swallowing
The esophagus is about 25 cm; peristalsis carries food to the stomach in roughly 9 seconds and works upside down (Straight Dope / standard physiology)
Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid, around pH 1.5-3.5; mucus and bicarbonate from foveolar cells protect the lining (Wikipedia: Foveolar cell)
Small intestine about 3-5 m in living adults; bile emulsifies fat, pancreatic juice neutralises acid; villi and microvilli; most nutrient absorption happens here (Wikipedia: Small intestine)
Gut lining surface ~32 m2, about half a badminton court, not a tennis court (Helander & Fändriks 2014, via PopSci)
About 6 hours through stomach and small intestine; up to 36-48 hours in the colon (Mayo Clinic)
About 38 trillion bacteria in the body, mostly in the colon (Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016)

topic.title: How did people in old Japan smell what time it was? (incense clocks)
topic.angle: Ukiyo-e Woodblock

package.title: The 1-Month Clock You Read With Your Nose
package.description:
How did people in old Japan and China tell time by smell? Incense clocks burned a trail of incense powder pressed into a maze in ash, and switching to a different incense at set marks meant the room's smell changed as time passed.

Sources:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incense_clock
https://museum.seiko.co.jp/en/knowledge/ElementalTimepieces03/
https://www.iflscience.com/in-medieval-china-and-japan-clever-devices-allowed-you-to-smell-what-time-it-is-83651

Animated in the Ukiyo-e Woodblock style.

Follow Zorbly AI for a new Short every day.
package.pinned_comment: If you had an incense clock, which smell would you want for the morning: pine, cedar or sandalwood?
package.script:
How did people in old Japan
smell what time it was?
No gears. No ticking.
Just a box of ash.
First, they smoothed white ash flat,
and pressed a stamp into it.
That left a groove,
a maze that snakes back and forth.
They filled the groove with incense powder:
one long, thin trail.
Light one end,
and a tiny ember crawls through the maze,
at a nearly steady speed.
Here's the clever part.
At set marks along the trail,
they switched to a different incense.
So when the smell in the room changed,
you knew more time had passed.
Some trails burned for twelve hours.
Some lasted a whole month.
A few even dropped a little ball
onto a tray, like an alarm.
So, what time does your room smell like right now?
key_facts: Seal-type incense clocks (Japanese ko-dokei) laid a continuous trail of incense powder in a pattern pressed into flattened ash with a stamp or stencil
The powder burned at a fairly steady rate, so elapsed time could be read from how far the ember had travelled
Markers or tablets of different incense placed along the trail changed the aroma when reached, so an attendant could tell the time by smell
Burn times ranged from about 12 hours to a month, depending on trail length
Some versions dropped balls into a tray when the incense burned through, as an audible signal
Incense clocks came to Japan from China and were used in Japan from the Nara period

topic.title: How does a plane toilet flush at 35,000 feet?
topic.angle: Synthwave Outrun

package.title: How a Plane Toilet Flushes at 35,000 Feet ✈️
package.description:
How does an airplane toilet flush? Plane toilets are vacuum toilets: a valve opens the bowl to the thin air outside, the higher cabin pressure shoves everything into a tank at the back, and below 16,000 feet an electric vacuum pump does the job instead.

Sources:
https://satelliteindustries.com/blog/vacuum-toilet-system-in-aircraft
https://thepointsguy.com/news/how-airplane-toilets-work/
https://aerocorner.com/blog/how-airplane-toilets-work/

Animated in the Synthwave Outrun style.

Follow Zorbly AI for a new Short every day.
tags: how does a plane toilet work
package.pinned_comment: Have you ever jumped when a plane toilet flushed? Be honest 😂
package.script:
How does a plane toilet flush
at thirty-five thousand feet?
It barely uses water.
It uses the sky.
Your cabin is pressurized,
packed with air like a balloon.
Outside, the air is super thin.
Press the button,
and a valve opens a pipe
from the bowl to that thin outside air.
The high pressure in the cabin
shoves everything down the pipe.
That's the whoosh.
It all lands in a tank at the back of the plane.
About three seconds later,
the valve slams shut.
But below sixteen thousand feet,
the outside air isn't thin enough,
so an electric pump makes the vacuum instead.
And no, nothing gets dumped in the sky.
Ground crews empty the tank after landing.
So, next flight,
are you brave enough to press it?
key_facts: Airplane toilets are vacuum toilets (patented by James Kemper in 1975, on Boeing jets by 1982)
At altitude a valve connects the bowl to low outside pressure; higher cabin pressure pushes waste through
Waste goes to a tank at the rear of the aircraft
Valves close after about 3-4 seconds
Below about 16,000 ft (and on the ground) an electric vacuum generator creates the suction
Waste is not dumped in flight; ground service trucks empty the tank after landing

tags: what happens to food after you eat
package.pinned_comment: Which food do you think takes the longest trip through your body? 🍙
package.script:
What actually happens to your food,
after you swallow it?
It's one of the longest trips in your body.
And for most of history,
nobody really knew how it worked.
Many ancient doctors thought the stomach
simply cooked your food, like a pot.
Then, in the seventeen hundreds,
scientists fed animals
food sealed inside little metal tubes.
The food couldn't be squished,
but it still dissolved.
Italian scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani
even tried it on himself,
swallowing tiny linen bags of food.
The answer was a liquid.
He called it gastric juice.
So let's follow one bite,
all the way through.
Step one: your mouth.
Your teeth crush the bite into mush,
and saliva soaks it.
Saliva holds an enzyme called amylase,
that starts turning starch into sugar,
before you even swallow.
Then your tongue pushes the food back,
and a tiny flap, the epiglottis,
folds down over your windpipe,
so nothing goes the wrong way.
Now the food enters the esophagus,
a muscle tube about twenty-five centimeters long.
It doesn't just fall.
Rings of muscle squeeze behind it,
like toothpaste in a tube.
That's called peristalsis.
The trip takes about nine seconds,
and it works even upside down.
Next stop, the stomach.
It's a stretchy bag of muscle,
filled with hydrochloric acid.
Stomach acid can drop to around pH two,
about as sour as lemon juice.
It kills a lot of germs,
and helps an enzyme called pepsin
start chopping up protein.
About three times a minute,
the stomach walls squeeze and churn,
mixing everything into a thick soup called chyme.
That can take two to four hours.
So why doesn't your stomach digest itself?
Its lining makes a thick coat of mucus,
plus bicarbonate to calm the acid.
And the lining cells get replaced every few days.
Then a little valve opens,
and lets the chyme out, a squirt at a time,
into the small intestine.
This is where the real magic happens.
It's about five meters long,
coiled up inside your belly.
Your liver sends in bile,
which breaks fat into tiny droplets.
Your pancreas adds more enzymes,
and neutralizes the acid.
The walls are covered in millions of tiny fingers,
called villi,
and those are covered in even tinier microvilli.
Spread flat, scientists estimate your gut lining
covers about thirty-two square meters.
That's half a badminton court!
Old textbooks said a whole tennis court,
but half a court is still huge.
Right here, most of the nutrients
slip into your blood.
What's left moves on to the large intestine.
It's wider, but only about one and a half meters long.
Its main job is soaking up water.
And it's home to trillions of bacteria.
Scientists estimate about thirty-eight trillion live in you,
mostly right here.
They munch the fiber you can't digest,
and make some vitamins in return.
So how long does the whole trip take?
About six hours through the stomach and small intestine,
and up to another two days in the large intestine.
Whatever your body can't use,
leaves at the end.
But the rest?
That bite became your energy,
your muscles,
even the thoughts you're having right now.
So which food do you think
takes the longest trip?
key_facts: Ancient physicians described digestion as 'concoction', a kind of cooking in the stomach; in the 1750s Réaumur fed a bird food in perforated metal tubes and the food still dissolved (Popular Science Monthly, 1909)
Lazzaro Spallanzani experimented on animals and himself in the 1770s-80s and named the stomach's solvent 'gastric juice' (whonamedit; Popular Science Monthly)
Saliva's amylase starts breaking starch into sugar; the epiglottis covers the windpipe during swallowing
The esophagus is about 25 cm; peristalsis carries food to the stomach in roughly 9 seconds and works upside down (Straight Dope / standard physiology)
Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid, around pH 1.5-3.5; mucus and bicarbonate from foveolar cells protect the lining (Wikipedia: Foveolar cell)
Small intestine about 3-5 m in living adults; bile emulsifies fat, pancreatic juice neutralises acid; villi and microvilli; most nutrient absorption happens here (Wikipedia: Small intestine)
Gut lining surface ~32 m2, about half a badminton court, not a tennis court (Helander & Fändriks 2014, via PopSci)
About 6 hours through stomach and small intestine; up to 36-48 hours in the colon (Mayo Clinic)
About 38 trillion bacteria in the body, mostly in the colon (Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016)

topic.title: Why do bats sleep upside down?

package.title: Why Bats Hang Upside Down for 20 Hours a Day 🦇
package.description:
Why do bats sleep upside down? Bats can't take off from the ground like birds, so they hang high up by their toes, let go and drop straight into flight, while a tendon lock in their feet keeps them hanging with zero muscle effort.

Sources:
https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/574568/why-do-bats-hang-upside-down
https://www.iowadnr.gov/news-release/2016-12-08/why-do-bats-hang-upside-down
https://www.scienceabc.com/nature/animals/revealed-why-do-bats-hang-upside-down-while-sleeping.html

Animated in the Cut-Paper Diorama style.

Follow Zorbly AI for a new Short every day.
tags: why do bats sleep upside down
how do bats hang upside down
package.pinned_comment: Could you nap upside down like a bat? How long do you think you'd last? 🦇
package.script:
You'd pass out sleeping upside down,
but some bats do it 20 hours a day.
So why hang like that?
Bats have a takeoff problem.
They're the only mammals that truly fly,
but their wings can't lift them off the ground,
and their back legs are too tiny to run.
So they sleep up high, hanging by their toes.
Time to go?
They let go, drop,
and they're flying before they hit anything.
But doesn't hanging all day get tiring?
Nope.
Their toe tendons work like a locking clip.
Body weight pulls the tendon tight,
and the claws clamp shut, with zero effort.
To let go, they use muscles to open them.
And the blood rush to the head?
Bats are so light, it barely happens.
Plus, up high, most predators can't reach them.
So, could you nap upside down like a bat?
key_facts: Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight
Bat wings can't generate enough lift from a standstill on the ground, and their hind legs are too small and light to run for a takeoff
Hanging lets them simply let go and drop into flight
Tendons in the feet are pulled tight by the bat's body weight, closing the claws with no muscle effort; muscles are needed to open them
Bats are light enough that blood pooling in the head is not a problem
Roosting high keeps them out of reach of most predators
Some species like the little brown bat sleep around 19-20 hours a day

topic.title: How do smoke detectors know there's a fire?
topic.angle: Flat-Vector Science

package.title: How Smoke Alarms Smell Smoke ☢️
package.description:
How does a smoke detector know there's a fire? Ionization smoke alarms use a speck of radioactive americium-241 to make the air carry a tiny current that smoke interrupts, while photoelectric alarms catch light scattered by smoke onto a hidden sensor.

Sources:
https://wx1.ans.org/pi/np/smoke
https://www.mentalfloss.com/technology/how-do-smoke-alarms-work
https://www.epa.gov/node/80409

Animated in the Flat-Vector Science style.

Follow Zorbly AI for a new Short every day.
tags: how does a smoke detector work
package.pinned_comment: Check the label on yours: does it say ionization (radioactive) or photoelectric (light)? Tell me which one you've got 👇
package.script:
Your smoke alarm might be radioactive.
Nobody tells you,
but that's how it smells smoke.
Inside sits a speck of americium,
which fires out tiny alpha particles.
They slam into the air
between two metal plates,
knocking electrons loose.
Now the air carries electricity,
so a tiny, steady current flows.
When smoke drifts in,
bits of smoke grab those charged particles.
The current drops,
and the alarm screams.
Other alarms use light instead.
An LED shines across a dark chamber,
away from a sensor.
No smoke, no light hits it.
But smoke scatters the beam,
bouncing light into the sensor.
Beep!
And that americium?
Its half-life is four hundred thirty-two years,
so it outlasts your alarm by centuries.
So, is the one above your bed
radioactive, or running on light?
key_facts: Ionization smoke alarms contain a small amount of americium-241, which emits alpha particles
Alpha particles ionize air between two electrodes, sustaining a small steady current
Smoke entering the chamber disrupts/reduces the current; below a threshold the alarm sounds
Photoelectric alarms shine an LED across a chamber away from a photocell; smoke scatters light onto the sensor
Americium-241 half-life is about 432 years (EPA: 432.2)
Smoke alarms are typically replaced about every 10 years

package.title: How Electricity Reaches Your Outlet in 4 Stops
package.description:
How does electricity get from the power plant to your outlet? Electricity explained in simple words: how a generator's spinning magnet makes alternating current, why step-up transformers push power lines up to 765,000 volts, how substations and pole transformers bring it down to 120 volts, and what the hot, neutral and ground holes in your outlet do.

Chapters:

0:17 Stop 1: The power plant
1:11 Stop 2: The voltage jump
1:52 Stop 3: The step back down
2:22 Stop 4: Your walls
2:52 The wildest part

Sources:
https://eli.lehigh.edu/support/electricity/electricity-generation-page-6
https://www.scienceabc.com/nature/what-is-the-speed-of-electricity.html
https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=105

Animated in the Synthwave Outrun style.

tags: how electricity gets to your house
package.pinned_comment: Before this video, did you think the electrons themselves raced from the power plant to your outlet? ⚡
package.script: Up to seven hundred sixty-five thousand volts flow through the biggest power lines, yet your outlet gives you just a hundred twenty. Here's how. It all starts with a spinning magnet, maybe hundreds of miles away. So let's follow the trip, in simple words. Stop one: the power plant. Almost every power plant does the same job. It spins something. Coal, gas and nuclear plants boil water into steam. Dams use falling water. Wind farms use, well, wind. All of it pushes the blades of a turbine, and the turbine spins a giant magnet inside coils of copper wire. Here's the trick, found by Michael Faraday back in 1831. When a magnet moves past a wire, it shoves the electrons inside that wire. Spin it nonstop, and you get a nonstop push. That push is electricity. And because the magnet keeps flipping north and south, the push swings back and forth too. In the US, it swings sixty times every second. In most of the world, it's fifty. That's called alternating current. Stop two: the voltage jump. A generator makes about twenty thousand volts. But right outside the plant, a step-up transformer cranks it way higher, up to seven hundred sixty-five thousand volts on the biggest lines. Why make it so extreme? Think of a garden hose. You can move a lot of water slowly through a fat hose, or the same water super fast through a thin one. Power lines work the same way. Crank the voltage up, and the current, the flow, drops way down. Less current means less heat wasted in the wires. Even so, about five percent of the power is lost as heat along the way. Stop three: the step back down. Seven hundred thousand volts would fry your toaster instantly. So the lines run into a substation, where big transformers drop it to a few thousand volts. Those smaller lines run down your street. Then one last transformer, that gray can on the pole, or a green box on the lawn, brings it down to what your house uses: a hundred twenty volts in the US, around two hundred thirty in much of the world. Stop four: your walls. The wire enters through a meter, which counts every bit you use, and then a breaker panel, which cuts the power if a wire gets too hot. From there, cables run to every outlet. And those holes aren't random. On a US outlet, the short slot is hot. That's where the push comes in. The tall slot is neutral, the path back. And the round hole is ground, a safety exit if something goes wrong. Now the wildest part. Flip a switch, and the light turns on instantly. But the electrons in the wire barely move. They crawl slower than a snail, mostly just wiggling back and forth. What races through the wire is the push itself, moving at close to the speed of light. So the energy in your charger left that spinning magnet a split second ago. Twenty thousand volts, then seven hundred sixty-five thousand, then down to the wall, all in the blink of an eye. Next time: if Earth is spinning so fast, why don't we fly off?
key_facts: Most power plants spin a turbine (steam from coal, gas or nuclear; falling water; wind) that turns a magnet inside copper coils; Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831
Grid power is alternating current: 60 Hz in the US, 50 Hz in most of the world
Generators put out roughly 20,000 volts (commonly cited 10,000-25,000); step-up transformers raise it to as much as 765,000 V on the biggest US lines
Higher voltage means lower current for the same power, so less is lost as heat; about 5% of US electricity is lost in transmission and distribution (EIA estimate)
Substations step down to a few thousand volts for distribution; pole-top or pad-mounted transformers bring it to 120/240 V in US homes (about 230 V in much of the world)
On a US outlet the shorter slot is hot, the taller slot is neutral and the round hole is ground
Electrons drift slowly (fractions of a millimetre per second) while the electrical signal/energy travels at a large fraction of the speed of light

topic.title: How was Velcro invented?
topic.angle: Chalkboard Lesson

package.title: How a Weed Invented Velcro in 1941 🤔
package.description:
How was Velcro invented? In 1941 Swiss engineer George de Mestral found burdock burrs stuck to his dog after a hike, saw tiny hooks under a microscope, and spent about ten years copying them in nylon hook-and-loop tape, patented in 1955.

Sources:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_de_Mestral
https://www.history.com/articles/velcro-invention

Animated in the Chalkboard Lesson style.

Follow Zorbly AI for a new Short every day.
package.pinned_comment: Be honest: when your Velcro shoes rip open, do you blame the weed or the dog? 👇
package.script:
A weed invented your Velcro,
in nineteen forty-one,
and almost nobody believed it.
A Swiss engineer, George de Mestral,
took his dog hiking in the Alps.
They came home covered in burrs,
the spiky seed heads of burdock.
Under a microscope,
every spike ended in a tiny hook,
and his clothes were full of tiny loops.
Hook meets loop,
and they grab on.
So he tried to copy it.
Cotton wore out too fast.
Nylon worked,
sewn under hot infrared light
into stiff little hooks.
It took him about ten years,
and the patent came in nineteen fifty-five.
He named it from two French words,
velours, for velvet,
and crochet, for hook.
Astronauts used it
to keep snack pouches from floating away.
So when your shoe straps rip open,
do you blame the weed, or the dog?
key_facts: In 1941, after a hunting trip in the Alps with his dog, George de Mestral found burdock burrs stuck to his clothes and the dog's fur
Under a microscope the burrs showed many tiny hooks that caught on loops in fabric and fur
Early cotton versions wore out quickly; nylon proved durable
Nylon hooks were formed by sewing nylon under hot infrared light
Development took about ten years; Swiss patent filed 1951, granted 1955
The name Velcro blends French velours (velvet) and crochet (hook)
NASA used Velcro on Apollo missions, including to hold food pouches in place in zero gravity

package.title: How Does a Pufferfish Puff Up? 🐡
package.description:
How does a pufferfish puff up? It gulps seawater into a folded, stretchy stomach that can expand up to 100 times, so its body balloons to about three times its size with spines sticking out.

Sources:
https://www.texassaltwaterfishingmagazine.com/fishing/education/science-sea/a-swell-adaptation
https://www.practicalfishkeeping.co.uk/fishkeeping-answers/how-do-pufferfish-inflate/
https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/60545/do-pufferfish-hold-their-breath-while-inflating-themselves

Animated in the Kawaii Anime style.

Follow Zorbly AI for a new Short every day.
tags: how does a pufferfish puff up
package.pinned_comment: If you could puff up like a pufferfish, what would make you do it? 🐡
package.script: A pufferfish stomach stretches 100 times bigger, and you'd never guess why it has to. When a hungry fish gets close, the pufferfish opens its mouth wide and gulps seawater, fast. Gulp after gulp, it pumps the water into its stomach. That stomach is folded like an accordion, so it unfolds and keeps on stretching. There are almost no ribs in the way, so the whole body balloons out. Its stretchy skin pulls tight, and little spines pop up all over. Now it's about three times its size, a spiky ball way too big to swallow. But puffing up is hard work. It can take hours to catch its breath, so it only puffs when it has to. Then it spits the water back out. So if you were a pufferfish, what would make you puff?
key_facts: Pufferfish inflate by gulping water into their stomach, not air (in water)
The folded stomach can expand roughly 50-100 times (Texas Saltwater Fishing Magazine)
Puffers lack ribs (or most ribs) and a pelvis, so the body can become a ball
Stretchy collagen-rich skin goes taut; spines stand up
Inflated balloonfish reach about 3x normal volume (3-4x per Mental Floss)
Recovery: heavy breathing for up to about 5 hours afterward (Mental Floss)

topic.title: Why don't giraffes faint when they lift their heads?
topic.angle: Cut-Paper Diorama

package.title: A Giraffe's 11 kg Heart Stops It Fainting 🦒
package.description:
Why don't giraffes faint when they lift their heads? A giraffe's brain sits about two meters above its heart, so it relies on an 11 kg heart pumping at about twice our blood pressure, one-way valves in its neck veins, and super-tight leg skin that works like compression socks.

Sources:
https://knowablemagazine.org/article/living-world/2021/heads-up-cardiovascular-secrets-giraffes
https://stanfordbloodcenter.org/for-giraffes-blood-circulation-is-a-tall-order/
https://repository.up.ac.za/handle/2263/13994

Animated in the Cut-Paper Diorama style.

Follow Zorbly AI for a new Short every day.
package.pinned_comment: If you had a giraffe's heart, do you think you'd ever get dizzy again? 🦒
package.script: You'd faint with your brain two meters up. Giraffes never do. Why? A giraffe swings its head from the water, all the way up to the treetops, and nothing happens. First, a monster heart. It weighs about eleven kilos, with walls thick enough to pump at twice your blood pressure. Second, valves in the neck veins. When the head drops down to drink, they stop blood flooding back into the brain. Third, scientists think the neck veins store blood, and when the head swings up, it rushes to the heart for one extra-strong beat. But all that pressure would make anyone's legs swell, so giraffes wear built-in compression socks: super-tight skin around their legs. So, if you had a giraffe's heart, would you still get dizzy with your brain two meters up?
key_facts: A giraffe's head sits about 2 m above its heart; head up to ~6 m above ground (Knowable Magazine)
Giraffe heart weighs about 25 lb / 11 kg (Stanford Blood Center)
Blood pressure at heart level ~220/180, roughly twice a human's (Knowable; Stanford)
Jugular vein valves stop backflow toward the brain when the head is lowered (Mitchell et al., Univ. of Pretoria)
Hypothesis: >1 L of blood pooled in neck veins returns to the heart when the head rises, giving a strong beat (Knowable, unconfirmed in awake giraffes)
Tight skin / dense connective tissue on the legs acts like support stockings (Knowable; Stanford)

package.title: Why Your Ears Pop at 8,000 Feet ✈️
package.description:
Why do your ears pop on a plane? A plane cabin is only pressurized to about 6,000 to 8,000 feet, so the air trapped behind your eardrum pushes out on the climb and gets squeezed in on landing until your 3.5 cm Eustachian tube opens and evens out the pressure.

Sources:
https://acibademinternational.com/blog/why-do-your-ears-pop-pressure-altitude-and-the-tube-that-fixes-it/
https://www.scienceabc.com/eyeopeners/ears-pop-airplane-takes-off-landing-air-pressure-difference
https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/13104/why-do-our-ears-pop-when-we-ride-airplanes

package.pinned_comment: Be honest: on landing, are you a yawner or a swallower? ✈️
package.script: A three and a half centimeter tube in your skull is why your ears pop. It's called the Eustachian tube, and it links your middle ear to the back of your throat. Behind your eardrum sits a tiny pocket of air. On the ground, it matches the air outside. But a plane cabin is only pressurized like an eight thousand foot mountain. So as you climb, the outside pressure drops, and the air behind your eardrum pushes out. Your eardrum bulges like a balloon, until the tube cracks open, air puffs out, and pop! Landing is trickier. Now the cabin air squeezes in, and that pressure pinches the tube shut. So you swallow, or you yawn. Tiny muscles yank the tube open, air rushes in, and your eardrum snaps back flat. So next flight, will you open that secret tube with a yawn, or a swallow?
key_facts: Adult Eustachian tube is about 3.5 cm long, linking the middle ear to the back of the nose/throat (Acibadem)
Airliner cabins are pressurized to roughly the pressure at 6,000-8,000 ft (Acibadem)
On the climb, higher pressure in the middle ear pushes the tube open from inside; the pop is pressure equalizing (Acibadem; Science ABC)
On descent, rising cabin pressure squeezes the tube shut so it must be actively opened (Acibadem; Science ABC)
Swallowing and yawning contract small soft-palate muscles that pull the tube open (Acibadem; Science ABC)
